payload.throughline: Follow fluid from blood to filtrate to urine, and label every movement by direction so nephron structure explains whole-body fluid, solute, pressure, pH, storage, and elimination effects.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: identify the direction of one lumen-to-blood transport step. This low-stakes check also activates the hard prerequisite V3-EDG-653998. If compartment flow, duct relationships, or absorption control from V3-LES-252091 is not ready, use the exact noncredit handoff before continuing.

Goal: map cortex, medulla, glomerulus, Bowman’s capsule, proximal tubule, loop, distal tubule, collecting duct, ureter, bladder, and urethra to fluid flow. The prerequisite handoff points specifically to V3-LES-252091 and its KCs V3-KC-507981, V3-KC-519155, and V3-KC-200171; it is not replaced by invented prerequisite teaching here.
Blood reaches a glomerular capillary tuft in the renal cortex. Filtered fluid crosses into Bowman’s capsule; blood cells and most large proteins remain in the circulation.

Filtrate then passes through proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, and collecting duct. Glomeruli and most proximal and distal tubule regions lie in the cortex, while loops and collecting ducts extend through the medulla.
Fluid that remains after nephron processing becomes urine and drains toward the ureter. The ureter carries urine to the bladder; the bladder stores it; the urethra carries it out.
Mental model: filter at the cortical cup, process along a cortex–medulla–cortex path, collect through the medulla, then convey, store, and eliminate.

Think aloud: a tracer has crossed from glomerular blood into Bowman’s space, so I now track tubular fluid—not blood. The next listed segment is proximal tubule, then loop, distal tubule, and collecting duct. Once it enters the ureter, I switch from nephron processing to urinary transport.
Worked example: a molecule appears in Bowman’s capsule and later in the descending limb. It must have passed through the proximal tubule before entering the loop.
A second tracer is already in the ureter. It has left nephron processing and will reach the bladder before the urethra.
Guided practice: place each structure on the visible route and mark whether the fluid is blood, filtrate, or urine at that point.
Less support: use cortex-versus-medulla location to identify a fresh structure.
On your own: select the next structure in a new flow description.

Boundary: the ureter and urethra are not interchangeable. Ureters carry urine from kidneys to bladder; the urethra carries urine from bladder outward. Also, blood does not flow through the tubular sequence.
Near exit: order a fresh set of nephron and urinary structures.
Changed-task exit: infer a damaged structure from where a tracer first stops along the route.
Repair the sequence function: split the route into filtration cup, tubular processing, and urinary transport. Rebuild each section before joining them.
Fresh near re-entry: order a different subset with no repeated option sequence.
Repair the localization function: identify the last reached compartment and the first missing downstream compartment. The boundary between them localizes the disrupted structure.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: localize a different obstruction using a new tracer path.
Recap: glomerulus to Bowman’s capsule starts filtrate flow; proximal tubule, loop, distal tubule, and collecting duct process it; ureter, bladder, and urethra transport, store, and eliminate urine.
Starting check: distinguish filtration from secretion. If the hard prerequisite’s compartment-flow model is not ready, the noncredit handoff to V3-LES-252091 remains available.

Goal: trace filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and countercurrent concentration through nephron regions. The lesson uses the exact prerequisite relation V3-EDG-653998 and does not invent a transporter or hormone catalog beyond packet scope.
Glomerular filtration moves water and small solutes from capillary blood into Bowman’s capsule. Cells and most large proteins remain in blood.

Reabsorption moves useful water and solutes from tubular fluid to peritubular capillary blood. Secretion moves selected substances from blood into tubular fluid. Excretion is what ultimately leaves as urine.

In the loop, the descending limb permits water loss, while the ascending limb removes salt but is relatively impermeable to water. This countercurrent arrangement builds a hyperosmotic medullary gradient that can draw water from collecting-duct fluid and concentrate urine.
Mental model: filter into the tube, reclaim out of the tube, secrete into the tube, then use a two-limb gradient to recover water before excretion.

Think aloud: if a solute moves from capillary to tubule after filtration, I label it secretion. For concentration, I look for opposite limb properties: water exits the descending limb; salt exits the ascending limb. Their countercurrent flow preserves the gradient.
Worked example: glucose is filtered into Bowman’s capsule and then moves from proximal tubular fluid back into capillary blood. The second movement is reabsorption.
As filtrate descends into a more concentrated medulla, water leaves. In the ascending limb, salt leaves without water, helping maintain the medullary gradient.
Guided practice: draw one arrow for blood-to-tubule or tubule-to-blood, then name the process.
Less support: use one limb property to predict whether tubular fluid becomes more dilute or concentrated.
On your own: infer the effect of disrupting one countercurrent step.

Boundary: filtration is not “all movement into a tubule.” It occurs at the glomerulus; later blood-to-tubule movement is secretion. The countercurrent multiplier is not simple passive equilibration because the two limbs have different transport properties.
Near exit: classify filtration, reabsorption, and secretion in a fresh nephron scenario.
Changed-task exit: infer how a lost ascending-limb salt gradient changes collecting-duct concentration.
Repair the transport-label function: name start and destination. Blood to Bowman’s space is filtration; tubule to blood is reabsorption; blood to tubule later is secretion.
Fresh near re-entry: classify a different solute movement with new compartments.
Repair the gradient function: the ascending limb establishes medullary salt concentration without following water. Weakening that step weakens the gradient available for downstream water recovery.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: predict urine concentration from a new descending-limb permeability disruption.
Recap: filtration starts tubular fluid, reabsorption returns selected material, secretion adds selected material, and countercurrent limb differences build the gradient used to conserve water.
Starting check: identify one consequence of failed water recovery. The exact prerequisite handoff remains available for learners who cannot yet track lumen-to-blood absorption.

Goal: predict renal effects on blood pressure, osmoregulation, acid–base balance, nitrogenous waste removal, water and solute recovery, storage, and elimination. Clinical renal management is outside scope.
Reabsorbing water and ions helps maintain blood volume and osmolarity; water recovery can therefore support blood pressure. Reabsorbing filtered glucose and amino acids conserves useful molecules.
Secretion of acid and handling of bicarbonate contribute to acid–base balance. Keeping nitrogenous wastes in tubular fluid and excreting them removes those wastes from the body.
Urine passes through ureters to the bladder for storage. During elimination, sphincter coordination permits urine to pass through the urethra.

Mental model: what returns to blood supports volume and useful solutes; what stays in or enters the tubule is available for waste and acid removal; the urinary tract then conveys, stores, and releases the final fluid.

Think aloud: if water reabsorption falls, more water remains in urine and less returns to blood. I predict higher urine volume and lower support for blood volume. If acid secretion falls, I focus on acid–base balance rather than storage anatomy.
Worked example: impaired glucose reabsorption leaves more glucose in tubular fluid, so more glucose appears in urine and less is recovered to blood.
A ureter obstruction affects conveyance from kidney to bladder; it does not relabel glomerular filtration or proximal reabsorption.
Guided practice: mark whether the affected substance returns to blood or remains for excretion, then predict one blood and one urine consequence.
Less support: infer the homeostatic category from a fresh transport defect.
On your own: trace a fluid or acid–base change through renal handling.

Boundary: urine storage in the bladder does not itself form or concentrate urine. Sphincters regulate elimination flow, not glomerular filtration. A transport defect and a urinary outflow obstruction therefore have different first consequences.
Near exit: predict a blood-and-urine consequence from altered renal recovery.
Changed-task exit: distinguish a nephron homeostasis defect from a urinary storage or outflow defect using observed data.
Repair the consequence function: write two destinations—back to blood or onward to urine. A decrease in reabsorption shifts the substance toward urine and away from blood recovery.
Fresh near re-entry: predict a new useful-solute recovery defect with no repeated substance or option structure.
Repair the localization function: altered composition points to nephron processing; normal composition with failed conveyance, storage, or release points to ureter, bladder, urethra, or sphincter.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: localize a different elimination defect from a new observation.
Recap: renal transport supports volume, osmolality, pH, nutrient recovery, and waste removal; ureters, bladder, urethra, and sphincters then convey, store, and release urine.
